moduli.nome: EGYPT, ANTI-COLONIALISM, THE MIDDLE EAST, AND AFRICA (Prof. Massimo Zaccaria)
argomenti: Module Description: Over the last twenty years, the history of the Cold War has undergone a significant renewal
In particular, two new perspectives have emerged: a stress on its global dimension and an emphasis on the diverse interrelationships between Cold War, Decolonization, and the rise of the Third World
Traditionally, the historiography focused primarily on the global competition between the two superpowers
Egypt’s history and geostrategic interests have shaped a country with multiple identities: its Arab identity has always gone hand in hand with an African one
As Nasser wrote in The Philosophy of the Revolution (1954), Egypt belonged to three worlds at once, the Arab, the African, and the Islamic, and he saw a role for his country in all three
In the 1950s and 1960s, Egypt sought to combine pan-Arabism, pan-Africanism, and anti-colonialism through an ambitious foreign policy

In particular, we shall be investigating problems of an ethical nature, problems that involve deciding what, in a moral sense, is the right thing to do
That states protect, but also violate, human rights
That conflicts, including armed conflicts, arise between states, and between groups within and across states
Such moral duties and claims might or might not turn out to coincide with the dictates of international law
They belong to the fields of moral and political philosophy
Human rights and international distributive justice
Are duties of global justice best understood as deriving from human rights?
Must egalitarian commitments necessarily be limited to the domestic sphere?
How, if at all, can a state come to have a moral right to govern and control a particular territory?
Are territorial rights like property rights in land?
What are the ethical grounds of national self-determination, and how do they relate to the grounds of territorial rights?
Is there a right of secession?
The right of free movement, and the rights and duties of states with respect to migrants
Is there a human right to freedom of movement?
When is a state morally justified in going to war?
Do civilians, soldiers, and terrorists differ in their degrees of moral immunity to attack or punishment?
